title: Chef's Kiss
desc: Regional feuds, forgotten superfoods & kitchen science gone wrong

questions.q: Carbonara traditionally uses guanciale — what cut of meat is that?
questions.a: Cured pork cheek (not bacon, not pancetta — Italians will fight you on this)

questions.q: What makes sourdough bread rise if there's no commercial yeast?
questions.a: Wild yeast and lactobacillus bacteria captured in the starter — they ferment naturally from the flour and environment

questions.q: The world's most expensive pizza costs over $12,000. What's on it?
questions.a: Varies by claim — but typically: buffalo mozzarella, lobster, caviar, and gold leaf. Some versions include three types of rare caviar

questions.q: In Japan, there's a high-end watermelon that regularly sells for how much?
questions.a: Up to $6,000 for a Densuke watermelon from Hokkaido — they only produce about 10,000 per year

questions.q: What gives Earl Grey tea its distinctive flavour?
questions.a: Bergamot oil — from a citrus fruit grown mostly in Calabria, Italy

questions.q: Brown eggs and white eggs taste different — true or false?
questions.a: False — the colour depends on the breed of chicken, not the taste or nutrition

questions.q: What ancient preservation technique involves burying food in ash and lye?
questions.a: Lutefisk — Nordic dried whitefish rehydrated in lye solution until gelatinous. Also: century eggs use a similar alkaline process

questions.q: Why does asparagus make some people's urine smell strange — and why can't everyone detect it?
questions.a: Asparagusic acid breaks down into sulphur compounds. About 40% of people lack the gene to smell them — the smell is there, they just can't perceive it

questions.q: Margherita pizza represents the Italian flag — red tomato, white mozzarella, green basil. But the story that it was invented for Queen Margherita is probably what?
questions.a: A myth — flatbreads with those toppings predated the supposed 1889 royal visit. The letter 'proving' it was likely forged

questions.q: What is the 'five-second rule' actually backed by in terms of science?
questions.a: Almost nothing — bacteria transfer is nearly instantaneous on contact. Moisture and surface type matter more than time
